(جُيُوبِهِنَّ): plural of jayb. The jayb of a shirt is its collar opening; [it also means] the heart and the breast. Among common people the jayb is a pocket sewn on the side of a garment on the inside, with its mouth made on the outside.
(أُولِي الْإِرْبَةِ): those having al-irba, and al-irba is need. In al-Miṣbāḥ:
"Al-arab, with two fatḥas, al-irba with kasra, and al-maʾraba with fatḥa or ḍamma on the rāʾ: need; the plural is al-maʾārib. Al-arab is originally a maṣdar of the pattern of taʿiba; one says ariba al-rajulu ilā al-shayʾ when he needs it, so he is āribun on the pattern of fāʿil. Al-irb with kasra is used for need and for a bodily member; the plural is ārāb, like ḥiml and aḥmāl."

* I'rab:
(قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصارِهِمْ وَيَحْفَظُوا فُرُوجَهُمْ): resumptive (mustaʾnaf) speech, brought to begin setting out general rulings comprehensive of all believers, within which the ruling on those asking permission when entering houses is wholly included. قل is an imperative verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; its object is omitted, being another command like it, omitted because its answer indicates it, namely يغضوا من أبصارهم. يغضوا is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) because it is the answer to the omitted command, which is غضّوا; or [the omitted command is] the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). من أبصارهم: al-Zamakhsharī said: "من is partitive, and what is meant is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and confining it to what is permitted. Al-Akhfash allowed that it be redundant (zāʾida), and Sībawayh rejected it." It may also be explicative (li-l-bayān) or for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya). In any case it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) يغضوا. The reason for من entering upon the gazes and not the private parts will come in the section on rhetoric. ويحفظوا is conjoined to يغضوا; فروجهم is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
(ذلِكَ أَزْكى لَهُمْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِما يَصْنَعُونَ): ذلك is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and أزكى its khabar (predicate); لهم is attached to أزكى; إنّ, its noun and its khabar; بما is attached to خبير; the clause يصنعون has no grammatical position.
(وَقُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِناتِ يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصارِهِنَّ وَيَحْفَظْنَ فُرُوجَهُنَّ): the i'rab of its counterpart has preceded; i.e. it is not lawful for a man to look at a woman nor for a woman to look at a man, for her attachment to him is like his attachment to her, and her desire for him like his desire for her. Among the curious things that catch the eye is that this verse contains a large number of feminine pronouns, their number reaching twenty-five pronouns, nominative and genitive; no parallel to it in this respect is found in the Qur'an.
(وَلا يُبْدِينَ زِينَتَهُنَّ إِلَّا ما ظَهَرَ مِنْها): the wāw is a conjunction; يبدين is conjoined to يغضضن, so it is indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn because of its connection with the nūn of the feminine plural, in the position of the jussive; the nūn is the agent; زينتهن is the direct object; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); ما is a badal (substitute) of زينتهن; the clause ظهر منها is the ṣila (relative clause). What is meant by the outward is the face and the two hands, so a stranger may look at them if he does not fear temptation, as is established in jurisprudence.
(وَلْيَضْرِبْنَ بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلى جُيُوبِهِنَّ): the wāw is a conjunction and the lām is the lām of command; يضربن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on sukūn in the position of the jussive by the lām; the nūn is the agent; بخمرهن: the bāʾ is redundant or partitive, i.e. let them cast their head-coverings over their collar openings, i.e. let them cover heads, necks and breasts with maqāniʿ, plural of miqnaʿa or miqnaʿ (with kasra on the mīm in both), which is what the head is covered with.
(وَلا يُبْدِينَ زِينَتَهُنَّ إِلَّا لِبُعُولَتِهِنَّ): the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; يبدين is an imperfect verb, indeclinable, in the position of the jussive; the nūn is the agent; زينتهن is the direct object; إلا is a particle of restriction; لبعولتهن is attached to يبدين. These excepted categories are twelve kinds, the last of them being the child.
(أَوْ آبائِهِنَّ أَوْ آباءِ بُعُولَتِهِنَّ أَوْ أَبْنائِهِنَّ أَوْ أَبْناءِ بُعُولَتِهِنَّ أَوْ إِخْوانِهِنَّ أَوْ بَنِي إِخْوانِهِنَّ أَوْ بَنِي أَخَواتِهِنَّ أَوْ نِسائِهِنَّ أَوْ ما مَلَكَتْ أَيْمانُهُنَّ): all of them are conjoined (maʿṭūfāt).
(أَوِ التَّابِعِينَ غَيْرِ أُولِي الْإِرْبَةِ مِنَ الرِّجالِ أَوِ الطِّفْلِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَظْهَرُوا عَلى عَوْراتِ النِّساءِ): غير is a naʿt (adjective) of التابعين. What is meant by "the followers without need" is a matter of disagreement. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the follower is the impotent fool. It is said: he is one who is not able to approach women and does not desire them; it is said: he is the majbūb; it is said: he is the decrepit old man whose desire has gone; and it is said: he is the effeminate (al-mukhannath). I say: and the impotent man, and the mukhannath is the one who resembles women, and the decrepit old man; as for the majbūb, he is the one whose testicles remain, and the eunuch (al-khaṣī) is the one whose penis remains.
[Translator's note: the sentence beginning "I say" is elliptical and apparently defective in the source; translated as written.]
من الرجال is a ḥāl (circumstantial); أو is a conjunction; الطفل is conjoined to what precedes; it means "children", the al being generic (jinsiyya); al-ṭifl is applied to the single and the plural, which is why it is qualified by a plural. It is also said: since the genus was intended, plurality was taken into account in it. الذين is a naʿt; the clause لم يظهروا is the ṣila; على عورات النساء is attached to يظهروا.
(وَلا يَضْرِبْنَ بِأَرْجُلِهِنَّ لِيُعْلَمَ ما يُخْفِينَ مِنْ زِينَتِهِنَّ): the wāw conjoins to what precedes; لا is prohibitive; يضربن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable, in the position of the jussive by لا; the nūn is the agent; بأرجلهن is attached to يضربن. A woman used to strike the ground with her foot so that her anklet would jingle and it would be known that she wore an anklet; it is also said that she used to strike one of her feet against the other so that it would be known that she wore two anklets. That breeds in men an inclination to them and gives the impression that they have an inclination to men. Al-Zajjāj said: "Hearing the sound of this adornment stirs desire more strongly than displaying it."
(وَتُوبُوا إِلَى اللَّهِ جَمِيعاً أَيُّهَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; توبوا is an imperative verb, indeclinable on the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the agent; إلى الله is attached to توبوا; جميعا is a ḥāl; أيها المؤمنون is a vocative, a specific indefinite (nakira maqṣūda), whose i'rab has preceded; لعلّ and its noun, and the clause تفلحون is its khabar. It [أيه] is written in the muṣḥaf without an alif, and the orthography is a followed practice.

* Rhetoric:
- Among the secrets that are too subtle for understanding is the entry of the preposition من upon the lowering of the gaze and not upon the private parts, in His words, Exalted is He, «قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصارِهِمْ وَيَحْفَظُوا فُرُوجَهُمْ». The secret of this is that the matter of looking is broad; the gaze never ceases to roam in the pastures of beauty and the places of temptation. Al-Zamakhsharī said in this connection: "Do you not see that there is no harm in looking at the hair, breasts, bosoms, upper arms, shins and feet of women within the forbidden degrees, and likewise slave-girls displayed for sale? Whereas the matter of the private parts is narrow."
- Among these secrets is the fronting of the lowering of the gaze before guarding the private parts, in this same verse and in the verse that follows it. The secret in it is that looking is the messenger of fornication and its scout that does not miss. Poets ancient and modern have expounded at length on how a glance kindles the fire of love and stokes the burning that drives one to commit what is forbidden. Among the finest things said about it is the saying of Ibn Zaydūn:
حسن أفانين لم تستوف أعيننا ... غاياته بأفانين من النظر
(A beauty of many kinds, whose utmost reaches our eyes could not exhaust with many kinds of gazing.)
And Ibn al-Rūmī said:
عيني لعينك حين تنظر مقتل ... لكن لحظك سهم حتف مرسل
ومن العجائب أن معنى واحدا ... هو منك لحظ وهو مني مقتل
(My eye, when it looks, is a mortal spot for your eye, but your glance is an arrow of death let fly; and among wonders is that one single thing is a glance from you and a mortal wound in me.)
Wonders of this will come in our book.
Below is a selection of the ḥadīths transmitted on this subject:
"From ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, meaning from his Lord: The glance is a poisoned arrow among the arrows of Iblīs; whoever abandons it out of fear of Me, I will replace it for him with faith whose sweetness he finds in his heart." I.e. I make in its place faith whose delights he feels in his heart.
[Translator's note: the source prints «من نركها», a misprint for «من تركها» (whoever abandons it).]
From Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:
"The son of Adam's share of fornication has been written for him, and he will inevitably attain it: the eyes — their fornication is looking; the ears — their fornication is listening; the tongue — its fornication is speech; the hand — its fornication is seizing; the foot — its fornication is the steps (al-khuṭā); and the heart desires and longs, and the private part confirms it or belies it." The meaning is that Allah the Exalted will punish the eye with fire on the Day of Resurrection for gazing at something forbidden deliberately, not by sudden chance. Al-khaṭā, with fatḥa on the khāʾ, is walking towards sin.
From ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Beware of entering upon women." A man of the Anṣār said: "What about the in-law (al-ḥam)?" He said: "The in-law is death." Al-Bukhārī and Muslim related it. Then he said:
The meaning of the disapproval of entering upon women is along the lines of what is related from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "No man is alone with a woman but that Satan is the third of them."
Al-ḥam — with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm without shadda, also with the wāw retained [ḥamū] and also with hamza [ḥamʾ] — is the husband's father and those related through him, such as the brother, the paternal uncle, the paternal cousin and the like; this is what is meant here, as al-Layth ibn Saʿd and others explained it. It is also the wife's father and those related through him. It is said, rather, that it is the husband's relative only, and it is said the wife's relative only. Abū ʿUbayd said concerning its meaning: i.e. let him die rather than do that. If this is a narration [i.e. view] about the husband's father, who is a maḥram, then what of a stranger? The meaning of "the in-law is death" is: fear from him is greater than from others, evil is expected from him, and the temptation greater, because he is able to reach the woman and be alone with her without anyone objecting to him.
[Translator's note: «فاذا كان هذا رواية في أب الزوج» is translated literally; «رواية» may be a misprint for «رأيه» (his view).]

dervis-irab:56-58.t:
* I'rab:
(وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ وَآتُوا الزَّكاةَ وَأَطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ) A statement conjoined to (وأطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول). Al-Zamakhsharī said:
"It is not far-fetched that a separator should come between the conjoined (maʿṭūf) and what it is conjoined to, even if long, because the right of the conjoined is to be other than what it is conjoined to." You may also conjoin it to an omitted [element] that the context requires, its implied form being: "So believe, do righteous deeds and establish the prayer." The parsing of the clause is entirely clear. (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَأْواهُمُ النَّارُ وَلَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ) (لا) is prohibitive; (تحسبن) is an imperfect verb indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, in the position of jussive by (لا); its fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you". (الذين) is the first object of (تحسبن); the clause (كفروا) is the ṣila (relative clause); (معجزين) is the second object of (تحسبن); (في الأرض) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial); and what (معجزين) is attached to is omitted, i.e. "[escaping] Us". (ومأواهم) is conjoined to (لا تحسبن الذين كفروا) — conjoining a declarative to an injunctive (ʿaṭf khabar ʿalā inshāʾ) — in the opinion of some of them; or it is conjoined to an implied [clause], its implied form being "rather they are overpowered [Translator's note: the source prints «مفهورون», evidently for «مقهورون», "overpowered"] and overtaken, and their refuge is…"; and perhaps this is better, because it is then conjoining a declarative to a declarative. (مأواهم) is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and (النار) its khabar (predicate), or the reverse. (ولبئس): the lām is the one that paves the way for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa lil-qasam); (بئس) is an inflexible (jāmid) past verb of blame; (المصير) is the fāʿil; and the one specified for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bil-dhamm) is omitted, i.e. "their destination", meaning the Fire. (يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِيَسْتَأْذِنْكُمُ الَّذِينَ مَلَكَتْ أَيْمانُكُمْ) A resumptive clause set out to explain the ruling on asking permission; more on it will come in the section on benefits. The lām is the lām of command; (يستأذنكم) is an imperfect verb made jussive by the lām of command; the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (الذين) is the fāʿil, and the clause (ملكت أيمانكم) is the ṣila. (وَالَّذِينَ لَمْ يَبْلُغُوا الْحُلُمَ مِنْكُمْ ثَلاثَ مَرَّاتٍ مِنْ قَبْلِ صَلاةِ الْفَجْرِ) (والذين) is conjoined to (الذين); the clause (لم يبلغوا الحلم) is the ṣila; (منكم) is a ḥāl. (ثلاث مرات) is accusative as an adverbial (ẓarf) or as a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object): if you take it in the sense of "three times (of day)" it is an adverbial, and if you take it in the sense of "three askings of permission" it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq. (من قبل صلاة الفجر) is a badal (substitute) of (ثلاث مرات); and it may be in the position of nominative as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. «هل من قبل» [Translator's note: so in the source; presumably «هي من قبل», "they are before…"]. Asking permission was made obligatory at that time only because it is the time of rising from beds and taking off the undergarments and the clothes in which one sleeps.
(وَحِينَ تَضَعُونَ ثِيابَكُمْ مِنَ الظَّهِيرَةِ) (وحين) is conjoined to the position of (من قبل صلاة الفجر); the clause (تضعون) is genitive by the adverb's being annexed to it; (ثيابكم) is the direct object; and (من الظهيرة) is a ḥāl, i.e. "at that time which is midday", or [it is attached] to (تضعون), so that (من) has the meaning of (في). (وَمِنْ بَعْدِ صَلاةِ الْعِشاءِ ثَلاثُ عَوْراتٍ لَكُمْ) (ومن بعد صلاة العشاء) is conjoined to what precedes it. (ثلاث عورات) is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, after which a muḍāf is implied, the muḍāf ilayhi having taken its place, i.e. "they are the times of three ʿawrāt". Each one of these states was called ʿawra because people's covering and guardedness are disturbed in them. Al-ʿawra is a gap (khalal). In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "aʿwara al-fāris: when a gap appears in the horseman for striking"; and al-aʿwar is one whose eye is defective.
(لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ وَلا عَلَيْهِمْ جُناحٌ بَعْدَهُنَّ طَوَّافُونَ عَلَيْكُمْ بَعْضُكُمْ عَلى بَعْضٍ) The clause (ليس عليكم…) is an adjective of (ثلاث عورات); the meaning is: they are three ʿawrāt specifically requiring permission. (عليكم) is the fronted khabar of laysa and (جناح) its postponed noun; (بعدهن) is an adverb attached to an omitted adjective of (جناح). (طوافون) is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "they"; (عليكم) is attached to (طوافون) because it is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha) of the active participle. (بعضكم) is a mubtadaʾ and (على بعض) its khabar, i.e. "going round to one another", indicated by (طوافون); and it may be parsed as a badal of His saying (طوافون). Abū Ḥayyān has a lengthy discussion on it of no use. (كَذلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الْآياتِ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ) The kāf is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun); this has preceded often. (يبين الله لكم الآيات) is an imperfect verb, its agent and its direct object; (الله) is a mubtadaʾ, (عليم) the first khabar and (حكيم) a second khabar.

* Benefits:
It is reported that Mudlij ibn ʿAmr, who was an Anṣārī boy, was sent by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at midday to ʿUmar to summon him. He went in to him while he was asleep and his garment had become uncovered from him. ʿUmar said: "I wish that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had forbidden our fathers, our sons and our servants to enter upon us at these hours except with permission." Then he went with him to the Prophet ﷺ and found that this verse had been revealed to him; it is one of the verses revealed on account of ʿUmar. It is also said it was revealed concerning Asmāʾ bint Abī Marthad, who said: "We enter upon the man and the woman, and perhaps they are under one blanket." It is also said: a grown boy of hers entered upon her at a time when she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
From Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: A man peeped in through one of the rooms of the Prophet ﷺ, so the Prophet ﷺ rose towards him with a mishqaṣ or mashāqiṣ — and it is as if I am looking at him stalking (yakhtil) the man to stab him. Narrated by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī, and its wording [in one version] is: "A Bedouin came to the door of the Prophet ﷺ and put his eye to a crack (khaṣāṣa) in the door. The Prophet ﷺ saw him and aimed at him (tawakhkhāhu) with a piece of iron or a stick to put out his eye. When he saw him, he withdrew. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'Had you stayed, I would have put out your eye.'"
Al-mishqaṣ: with kasra on the mīm, followed by a vowelless shīn and a qāf with fatḥa; it is an arrow with a broad head — it is also said a long one — and it is also said to be the broad arrowhead itself, and it is said the long one.
Yakhtiluhu: with kasra on the tāʾ, i.e. he deceives him and outmanoeuvres him.
Khaṣāṣat al-bāb: with fatḥa on the dotted khāʾ and two undotted ṣāds; it is the hole in it and the cracks. Its meaning is that he placed the crack in the door opposite his eye.
Tawakhkhāhu: i.e. he aimed at him; with a doubled dotted khāʾ.

dervis-irab:32-33.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْأَيامى): plural of ayyim, which is a woman who has no husband, whether virgin or previously married, and a man who has no wife. This is among free men and free women, as indicated by His words وإمائكم. Ayyim is also pluralised as ayāʾim, ayyimūn and ayyimāt. One says āma, yaʾīmu: a man [became unmarried] from his wife, or a woman from her husband, i.e. he lost her or she lost him. The original form of al-ayāmā is ayāʾim, as al-Zamakhsharī said, and similar to it is yatāmā from yatāʾim; Sībawayh allowed that it not be metathesised (maqlūb), being a plural on the pattern faʿālā. The poet said:
فإن تنكحي أنكح وإن تتأيمي ... وإن كنت أفتى منكم أتأيم
(If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried — even though I am younger than you — I will remain unmarried.)
He says to his beloved: if you marry I will marry, and if you do not marry I will not marry. The clause وإن كنت أفتى منكم is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya); al-aftā is the more youthful. Putting the imperfect in the nominative in the apodosis of a condition, as here, is rare; it has occurred in poetry when the protasis is a past verb, as here.
[Translator's note: in the verse as printed, the apodosis verbs «أنكح» and «أتأيم» carry no visible nominative marking and the protasis verbs are imperfect, not past; the comment is translated as written.]
And in the ḥadīth: «اللهم إني أعوذ بك من العيمة والغيمة والأئمة والكزم والقرم» (O Allah, I seek refuge in You from al-ʿayma, al-ghayma, al-ayma, al-kazam and al-qaram). Al-ʿayma is intense craving for milk; al-ghayma is intense craving from thirst; al-ayma is prolonged celibacy; al-kazam is intense craving for food — he said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: kazama al-shayʾa bi-muqaddami fīhi, i.e. he broke it [with his front teeth] and extracted what was in it; and al-qaram is intense craving for meat.
[Translator's note: the source spells the third word «الأئمة», evidently for «الأيمة» (al-ayma), the sense required by the explanation.]
(الْكِتابَ): al-kitāb and al-mukātaba, like al-ʿitāb and al-muʿātaba: it is that a man says to his slave, "I have contracted with you (kātabtuka) for a thousand dirhams," and if he pays them he is freed. Its meaning is: I have written for you, binding on myself, that you are freed from me if you pay the money, and you have written for me, binding on yourself, that you will pay it; or: I have written for you [the obligation of] paying the money, and written upon myself the freeing. It has rulings set out at length in the books of jurisprudence. In al-Asās and al-Lisān: "Kutiba ʿalayhi kadhā: it was decreed for him. Allah wrote [decreed] the term and the provision, and wrote obedience upon His servants and mercy upon Himself; and this is the kitāb of Allah: His decree." Al-Jaʿdī said:
يا بنت عمي كتاب الله أخرني ... عنكم وهل أمنعن الله ما فعلا
(O my cousin, Allah's decree has kept me back from you; and can I prevent Allah from what He has done?)
(الْبِغاءِ): fornication (al-zināʾ). Baghat so-and-so (fem.) bighāʾan, and she is a baghiyy: one who seeks men; they are baghāyā. From this slave-girls were called al-baghāyā, because they used to fornicate (yubāghīna) in the Jāhiliyya; one says: the baghāyā stood at their heads [serving them]. Al-Aʿshā said:
والبغايا يركضن أكسية الاضريج والشّرعبيّ ذا الأذيال
(And the slave-girls kick out the hems of robes of yellow silk and long-trailing Sharʿabī cloth.)
And in al-Miṣbāḥ: "Baghat al-marʾa, tabghī, bighāʾan (with kasra and lengthening), of the pattern of ramā: she committed lewdness; she is a baghiyy, plural al-baghāyā. It is a description specific to women; one does not say baghiyy of a man — al-Azharī said it. Al-baghiyy is also the singing slave-girl (al-qayna), even if she is chaste, because lewdness was originally established for her — al-Jawharī said it — and it is not meant as an insult, because it is a name made like a title. And the slave-girl tubāghī, i.e. fornicates."

* I'rab:
(وَأَنْكِحُوا الْأَيامى مِنْكُمْ وَالصَّالِحِينَ مِنْ عِبادِكُمْ وَإِمائِكُمْ): the wāw is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to establish the ruling on marriage. The command is for obligation if the woman needs marriage for fear of fornication or the man needs marriage for fear of fornication; if there is no such need, the command is for permissibility, as al-Shāfiʿī held, or for recommendation, as Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik held; the details are in the books of jurisprudence. الأيامى is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); منكم is a ḥāl (circumstantial); والصالحين is conjoined to الأيامى; من عبادكم is a ḥāl; وإمائكم is conjoined to عبادكم.
(إِنْ يَكُونُوا فُقَراءَ يُغْنِهِمُ اللَّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ وَاللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ): إن is conditional; يكونوا is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); the wāw is its noun and فقراء its khabar (predicate); يغنهم الله is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); من فضله is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) يغنهم; الله is a mubtadaʾ (subject), واسع a first khabar and عليم a second khabar.
(وَلْيَسْتَعْفِفِ الَّذِينَ لا يَجِدُونَ نِكاحاً حَتَّى يُغْنِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ): the wāw is a conjunction and the lām is the lām of command; يستعفف is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command; الذين is the fāʿil (agent); the clause لا يجدون is the ṣila (relative clause); نكاحا is the direct object; حتى is a particle of limit and a preposition; يغنيهم is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after حتى; الله is the agent; من فضله is attached to يغنيهم.
(وَالَّذِينَ يَبْتَغُونَ الْكِتابَ مِمَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمانُكُمْ فَكاتِبُوهُمْ إِنْ عَلِمْتُمْ فِيهِمْ خَيْراً): الذين is accusative by ishtighāl (preoccupation), i.e. accusative by an implied verb which the mentioned one explains. It may also be parsed as a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the clause فكاتبوهم; the first is preferable because of the command. The clause يبتغون الكتاب is the ṣila; مما is a ḥāl; the clause ملكت أيمانكم is a ṣila; the fāʾ is the connective because of the scent of condition in the relative noun; كاتبوهم is an imperative verb, the wāw being the agent; the clause is explicative (mufassira) on the first view and a khabar on the second. إن is conditional; علمتم is a past verb and its agent, in the position of the jussive as the protasis; فيهم is attached to علمتم; خيرا is the direct object; and the apodosis is omitted, indicated by His words فكاتبوهم.
(وَآتُوهُمْ مِنْ مالِ اللَّهِ الَّذِي آتاكُمْ): وآتوهم is conjoined to فكاتبوهم; من مال الله is attached to آتوهم; الذي is a naʿt (adjective) of الله [sic]; the clause آتاكم is the ṣila of the relative.
[Translator's note: «الذي» grammatically qualifies «مال», not «الله»; the source's wording «صفة لله» is translated as written.]
(وَلا تُكْرِهُوا فَتَياتِكُمْ عَلَى الْبِغاءِ إِنْ أَرَدْنَ تَحَصُّناً لِتَبْتَغُوا عَرَضَ الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا): the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تكرهوا is an imperfect verb, jussive by prohibitive لا; على البغاء is attached to تكرهوا; إن is conditional; أردن is a past verb and its agent, in the position of the jussive as the protasis; تحصنا is a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose) [sic]; and the apodosis is omitted, as has preceded. لتبتغوا: the lām is causal; تبتغوا is an imperfect verb, accusative by an implied أن after the causal lām; the wāw is the agent; عرض الحياة الدنيا is the direct object.
[Translator's note: «تحصنا» is the object of «أردن»; the source's «مفعول له» is translated as written and may be a slip for «مفعول به».]
(وَمَنْ يُكْرِهْهُنَّ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ مِنْ بَعْدِ إِكْراهِهِنَّ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ): the wāw is a conjunction; من is a jussive-governing conditional noun, a mubtadaʾ; يكرههن is the protasis; the fāʾ is the connective because the apodosis is a nominal clause; إنّ and its noun; من بعد إكراههن is a ḥāl; غفور is the first khabar of إنّ and رحيم its second khabar.

* Rhetoric:
Precaution (al-iḥtirās): in His words, Exalted is He, «إِنْ أَرَدْنَ تَحَصُّناً». This parenthesis was inserted to make the matter appear hideous to the addressee and warn him against falling into it, and so that he would wake up to the fact that he ought to disdain this vice even if there were no legal deterrent. The aspect of hideousness against him is that the content of the verse proclaims about him that his slave-girl is better than he, because she preferred chastity over indecency while he insists on nothing but forcing her. Abū al-Suʿūd has a fine statement on this subject: "His words, Exalted is He, 'if they desire chastity', are not for restricting the prohibition to the case of their desiring to refrain from fornication and excluding other cases from its ruling — as when the compulsion is because of their dislike of fornication with a particular fornicator, or at a particular time, or in a particular place, or for other such things that would make compulsion valid in some sense — but rather to reflect their continual custom, for they used to compel them to prostitution while they wanted to refrain from it, despite the abundance of their desire, which commands to lewdness, and their deficiency in knowing the matters that call to virtues and deter from engaging in vile deeds."
It is useful to mention the cause of revelation of this verse. They have mentioned that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, who used to compel his slave-girls to earn by fornication. They were six, and two of them complained to the Prophet ﷺ, so the verse was revealed. The names of these slave-girls were: Muʿādha, Musayka, Umayma, ʿAmra, Arwā and Qutayla.

* Benefits:
From ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O company of young men, whoever among you is able to afford al-bāʾa, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze more and guards the private part better; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a wijāʾ (restraint) for him." Al-Bukhārī and Muslim related it.
He singled out young men only because the strength of the urge to marriage is predominantly found in them, unlike old men. Al-bāʾa is sexual intercourse, and it has been used for the marriage contract. Al-Jawharī said: al-bāʾa is like al-bāʿa, and from it marriage was called bāʾa. The original meaning of al-wijāʾ is crushing the testicles. Al-Nawawī said in his commentary on Muslim: "Its meaning is: whoever among you is able to have intercourse because he can bear its costs, namely the costs of marriage, let him marry; and whoever is not able to have intercourse because he is unable to bear its costs, let him fast, to cut off his desire and cut off the evil of his semen as wijāʾ cuts it off." There is another view, namely that what is meant by al-bāʾa is the costs of marriage, named by the name of what accompanies them; its implied meaning is: whoever among you can bear the costs of marriage, let him marry, and whoever cannot, let him fast. They said: the one who is [physically] incapable does not need fasting to repel desire, so al-bāʾa must be interpreted as the costs.

dervis-irab:59-61.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَالْقَواعِدُ): plural of qāʿid, without tāʾ [marbūṭa]. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "The woman has ceased (qaʿadat) from menstruation: she has grown old and her menses have stopped, so she is qāʿid, without tāʾ, and the plural is qawāʿid; and she has ceased from [desire for] a husband, so she does not desire him." Were it not for their being specified with this [meaning], the tāʾ would be required, as in ḍāriba, and qāʿida from the well-known [sense of] sitting.
(مُتَبَرِّجاتٍ): displaying adornment. The reality of tabarruj is taking pains to display what ought to be concealed, from their saying "safīna bārij": a ship with no covering on it. Al-baraj, with vowelled letters, is the wideness of the eye, whereby its white is seen surrounding all of its black, nothing of it being hidden. However, it became specific to a woman's exposing herself to men by revealing her adornment and displaying her charms to men. In al-Mukhtār: "al-tabarruj is a woman's displaying her adornment and charms to men." Al-baraj conveys the meaning of wideness: it is said barija yabraju barajan, of the pattern of taʿiba, [meaning] his affairs became ample in eating, drinking and the like; and his eye became wide (barijat), such that its white is seen encircling all of the black. Al-burj is the corner, the fortress, the palace, and every elevated building of round or square shape, whether standing alone or part of a great building; its plural is buruj (with two ḍammas), abrāj and abrija. Al-burj is also one of the constellations of the sky, which are twelve: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces. Al-bārija is a large ship for fighting, and its plural is bawārij. Among their sayings: "so-and-so is nothing but a bārija, in which all evil has been gathered", i.e. he is wicked.
(صَدِيقِكُمْ): al-ṣadīq may be singular or plural, and likewise al-khalīṭ, al-qaṭīn and al-ʿaduww. It is the one true in affection and close friendship. The poet said:
دعون الهوى ثم ارتمين قلوبنا ... بأعين أعداء وهن صديق
(They summoned love, then shot at our hearts with the eyes of enemies, while they are friends.)
From here Abū Nuwās stole its meaning in his saying:
إذا امتحن الدنيا لبيب تكشفت ... له عن عدو في ثياب صديق
(When a wise man tests the world, it reveals to him an enemy in the clothes of a friend.)
(أَشْتاتاً): plural of shatt, meaning dispersal. In al-Mukhtār: "amrun shattun, with fatḥa, i.e. scattered. You say: shatta al-amru yashittu, with kasra, of the pattern of ḍaraba, shattan and shatātan, with fatḥa on the shīn in both, i.e. it became scattered."

* I'rab:
(وَإِذا بَلَغَ الْأَطْفالُ مِنْكُمُ الْحُلُمَ فَلْيَسْتَأْذِنُوا كَمَا اسْتَأْذَنَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ) A resumptive statement set out to establish the ruling on children who have passed the bounds of childhood by having wet dreams or reaching the age at which puberty is ruled, regarding the obligation of asking permission. (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition; the clause (بلغ الأطفال) is genitive by (إذا)'s being annexed to it; (منكم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); (الحلم) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the fāʾ links the answer of (إذا); the lām is the lām of command; (يستأذنوا) is an imperfect made jussive by the lām. (كما) is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), and (ما) is maṣdariyya, i.e. "an asking of permission like the asking of permission of those before them"; (الذين) is the fāʿil (agent) and (من قبلهم) is attached to (mutaʿalliq) the ṣila (relative clause). (كَذلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ آياتِهِ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ) The kāf is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar; (يبين الله) is an imperfect verb and its agent; (لكم) is attached to (يبين); (آياته) is the direct object; (الله) is the mubtadaʾ (subject), (عليم) the first khabar (predicate) and (حكيم) a second khabar. (وَالْقَواعِدُ مِنَ النِّساءِ اللَّاتِي لا يَرْجُونَ نِكاحاً) The wāw is resumptive; (القواعد) is a mubtadaʾ; (من النساء) is a ḥāl; (اللاتي) is an adjective of (القواعد), not of (النساء), since [otherwise] there would remain no justification for the fāʾ entering the khabar of the mubtadaʾ. The clause (لا يرجون) is the ṣila; (يرجون) is an imperfect verb indeclinable (mabnī) on the sukūn because of its attachment to the nūn of the feminine plural, the nūn being the fāʿil; and (نكاحا) is the direct object.
(فَلَيْسَ عَلَيْهِنَّ جُناحٌ أَنْ يَضَعْنَ ثِيابَهُنَّ غَيْرَ مُتَبَرِّجاتٍ بِزِينَةٍ) The fāʾ falls in the answer to the relative, because the alif-lām in (القواعد) has the meaning of "those women who have ceased". The clause (ليس) is the khabar of (القواعد); (عليهن) is the fronted khabar of laysa and (جناح) its postponed noun. (أن) and what falls within its scope are in the position of accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "in that they lay aside their garments", meaning take off their [outer] garments, so that it is permitted to look at their hands and faces. Further elaboration of this verse will come in the section on rhetoric. (غير متبرجات) is a ḥāl, and (بزينة) is attached to (متبرجات). Some considered it [the bāʾ] in the sense of the lām, i.e. "not displaying for adornment", and others considered the bāʾ to be for making transitive (taʿdiya), i.e. "not displaying adornment".
In the gloss of al-Shihāb on al-Bayḍāwī: "His saying 'not displaying adornment': by it he indicated that the bāʾ is for making transitive; that is why he explained it with a transitive [verb], although explaining an intransitive with a transitive is common. It is supported by the fact that the lexicographers did not mention it as transitive by itself, and we have not seen anyone say 'tabarrajat al-marʾatu ḥulyahā' (the woman displayed her jewellery). Nor is adornment taken into its concept, so that it could be said that it is a stripping [of part of the meaning] (tajrīd), as has been imagined. So whoever said that it indicates that the bāʾ is redundant (zāʾida) in the direct object has erred."
(وَأَنْ يَسْتَعْفِفْنَ خَيْرٌ لَهُنَّ وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ) The wāw is a conjunction; (أن) and what falls within its scope are the mubtadaʾ; (خير) is the khabar and (لهن) is attached to (خير), i.e. "and refraining from laying aside is better for them." Having mentioned what is permissible, He followed it with what is recommended, urging the choice of the best and finest of deeds, as in His saying «وأن تعفوا أقرب للتقوى» and «وأن تصدقوا خير لكم». (الله) is a mubtadaʾ, (سميع) the first khabar and (عليم) a second khabar. (لَيْسَ عَلَى الْأَعْمى حَرَجٌ وَلا عَلَى الْأَعْرَجِ حَرَجٌ وَلا عَلَى الْمَرِيضِ حَرَجٌ) A resumptive statement set out for a matter on whose interpretation the scholars differed. The nearest of the interpretations they mentioned is that these three groups used to feel awkward about eating with the healthy: for the blind man's hand may reach the best of the food first and so get to it before the seeing; the lame man spreads himself out in his sitting and takes a wide place, crowding the sound one; and the sick man is not free of a state that harms his companion and the one sitting with him. So this verse was revealed. The rest of the views will come in the section on benefits.
(ليس) is a defective past verb; (على الأعمى) is its fronted khabar and (حرج) its postponed noun; (ولا على الأعرج حرج) is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise what comes after it.
(وَلا عَلى أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَنْ تَأْكُلُوا مِنْ بُيُوتِكُمْ) The wāw is resumptive, and what follows it is a resumptive statement to establish the permissibility of what they had forbidden themselves. In al-Qurṭubī: "When Allah revealed «يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تأكلوا أموالكم بينكم بالباطل», the Muslims said: Allah has forbidden us to consume our wealth among ourselves unjustly, and food is among the best of wealth, so it is not lawful for any of us to eat at anyone's [house]. Then [this] was revealed." (لا) is negative; (على أنفسكم) is a fronted khabar; (أن) and what falls within its scope are a postponed mubtadaʾ; and (من بيوتكم) is attached to (تأكلوا). (أَوْ بُيُوتِ آبائِكُمْ أَوْ بُيُوتِ أُمَّهاتِكُمْ أَوْ بُيُوتِ إِخْوانِكُمْ) Conjoined to what preceded; (إخوانكم) has the meaning of (إخوتكم). (أَوْ بُيُوتِ أَخَواتِكُمْ أَوْ بُيُوتِ أَعْمامِكُمْ أَوْ بُيُوتِ عَمَّاتِكُمْ) Also conjoined to what preceded.
(أَوْ بُيُوتِ أَخْوالِكُمْ أَوْ بُيُوتِ خالاتِكُمْ) Also conjoined to what preceded.
(أَوْ ما مَلَكْتُمْ مَفاتِحَهُ أَوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ) (ما) is conjoined to what preceded; the clause (ملكتم) is the ṣila; (مفاتحه) is the direct object. What is meant by it is a man's wealth when he has over it a steward or agent who guards it for him. (المفاتح) is the plural of miftaḥ, and it is [also] pluralised as mafātīḥ; what is meant is the storehouses. (أو) is a conjunction and (صديقكم) is conjoined to what preceded. (لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُناحٌ أَنْ تَأْكُلُوا جَمِيعاً أَوْ أَشْتاتاً) The clause is a badal (substitute) of the previous clause. (أن تأكلوا): (أن) and what falls within its scope are accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "in that you eat"; (جميعا) is a ḥāl and (أشتاتا) is conjoined to (جميعا). The meaning is that, when they felt awkward about gathering for food and sharing in it because of the differences among those eating, He made clear that there is no blame on them in eating together or separately. Further elaboration of all this will come in the two sections of rhetoric and benefits. (فَإِذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتاً فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أَنْفُسِكُمْ تَحِيَّةً مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ مُبارَكَةً طَيِّبَةً) The fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition; the clause (دخلتم) is in the position of genitive by the adverb's being annexed to it; (بيوتا) is accusative as an object by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa). There is disagreement over what is meant by these houses; the correct view is that they are general, since there is no evidence of specification. (فسلموا): the fāʾ is linking; (سلموا) is an imperative verb and its agent; (على أنفسكم) is attached to (سلموا). (تحية) is accusative as a maṣdar from the meaning of (فسلموا), being its synonym, as in «قعدت جلوسا» and «فرحت جذلا» [Translator's note: the source prints «جزلا»]. (من عند الله) is an adjective of (تحية), or [attached] to the word (التحية) itself; (مباركة) is an adjective and (طيبة) is also an adjective, i.e. by which increase of good is hoped for and by which the soul of the hearer is pleased. (كَذلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمُ الْآياتِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ) The kāf is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar; (يبين الله) is an imperfect verb and its agent; (لكم) is attached to (يبين); (الآيات) is the direct object; laʿalla and its noun, and the clause (تعقلون) is the khabar of laʿalla.

* Rhetoric:
1- Reversal of the apparent (ʿaks al-ẓāhir):
In His saying, Exalted is He, «غير متبرجات بزينة» there is a device that some scholars of bayān call "reversal of the apparent" (ʿaks al-ẓāhir), and some call "negating a thing by affirming it" (nafy al-shayʾ bi-ījābih). It has been alluded to before in our book, and it is among the beauties of speech: when you reflect on it, you find its inner sense to be negation and its outward form affirmation; or [it is] that you mention speech whose apparent sense indicates that it negates a quality of something described, while it is a negation of the thing described altogether. Among its most important verses is the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
على لاحب لا يهتدى بمناره ... إذا سافه العود النباطي جرجرا
(Upon a clear, beaten track whose waymarks give no guidance; when the old, huge camel sniffs it, it groans.)
Al-lāḥib is the clear road; al-manār is the sign set on the road for guidance — and in the ḥadīth: "Religion has waymarks and signs like the signs of the road" —; sāfahu: sniffed it; al-ʿawd: the old camel; al-nabāṭī: the huge one; jarjara: it bellowed, clamoured and brought up its cud. By his saying «لا يهتدى بمناره» he did not mean that it has waymarks by which no guidance is found; rather he meant that it has no waymarks by which guidance could be found.
Likewise what is meant here: "the women past childbearing who have no adornment with which to display themselves", because the discussion concerns one who is in this condition. It is as if the purpose of this is that, for these women, refraining from laying aside garments is better for them — so what do you think of those who possess adornment in garments? The most eloquent thing in this is that He made not laying aside garments, in the case of the elderly women, part of chastity (istiʿfāf), signalling that laying aside garments has no place in chastity. This is for the elderly women — so how about the young, full-breasted ones?!
2- Clarification (al-īḍāḥ):
In His saying «ولا على أنفسكم» (the verse) there is the device of īḍāḥ (clarification), which is that the speaker mentions speech that outwardly contains ambiguity and then clarifies it in the rest of his speech. The difficulty that īḍāḥ resolves lies in the meanings of the rare words (al-badīʿ min al-alfāẓ), in their parsing, and in the intrinsic meanings rather than the [rhetorical] devices. It has been mentioned earlier in this book. Here in this verse, questions arise on its apparent sense. The first: what is the benefit of announcing the removal of blame from one who eats from his own house? How could one think that there is blame on one who eats from his own house?
The second: why did He not mention the houses of children, as He mentioned the houses of others among close relatives?
The third: what is the benefit of His saying «أو ما ملكتم مفاتحه», when apparently this is included in His saying «من بيوتكم»? The fourth: how did the equation between the friend and these relatives come about?
The answers by which these four difficulties are clarified are:
The first answer:
As for the benefit of announcing the removal of blame from one who eats from his own house, He mentioned that only as a preparation, to build upon it what He conjoins to its clause of houses from which He intended to permit eating. For if it is known that a person bears no blame in eating from his own house, likewise he bears no blame in eating from these houses — to indicate that the wealth of these relatives is like a person's own wealth. And if these [kinds of] wealth are equal, that equality extends to the spouses. So He, Glorified is He, has embedded in this (adhmaja) an exhortation to maintain ties of kinship and to treat them as a person treats himself.
The second answer:
As for not mentioning the houses of children: He mentioned only such wealth as might be thought forbidden to eat from, so it needed a statement of permissibility. As for the children's wealth, the parents' disposal of it is like their disposal of their own wealth, because a man's child is part of him and its ruling is the ruling of himself. Do you not see that the Sharia obliges the child to maintain the parents if they are needy? And in the ḥadīth: "The best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings."
The third answer:
As for the claim of the one who says that the speech contains overlap, because His saying «أو ما ملكتم مفاتحه» is what is in their houses: it is possible that by what is in the houses is meant inherited, long-held wealth, and by what a person owns the keys of, newly acquired wealth, which a person works to obtain and toils to earn.
The fourth answer:
As for the secret of equating the friend with these relatives, it is to make known the right of the friend whose inner self equals his outer self in sincerity of affection — and he is not called a friend until he is so, for the derivation of his name is from truthfulness of love (ṣidq al-maḥabba) and purity of affection; and he is the one to whom He, Glorified is He, alluded in His saying «ولا صديق حميم». So if the friend is of this standing and this description, he is equal to these close relatives, and there is no blame on a person if he disposes of his wealth as he disposes of his own wealth.
Other devices in the noble verse:
Further, this noble verse — some clarification of these difficulties [Translator's note: so in the source, «بعض إيضاح»; presumably «بعد إيضاح», "after the clarification of"] — contains nine kinds of the devices of badīʿ, which we list below in summary and brief form:
a- Ṣiḥḥat al-taqsīm (sound division): because the speech comprehends all categories of close relatives, such that it left none of them out.
b- Al-tahdhīb (refinement): in the progression of the speech according to what eloquence requires in this place, for eloquence requires placing first the nearest, then the next nearest, as came in it.
c- Ḥusn al-nasaq (beautiful arrangement): in His choice of «أو» to conjoin the clauses, which indicates permissibility.
d- Al-kināya (metonymy): He, Glorified is He, alluded to wealth by houses, which are the safekeeping of wealth and its place, by way of naming a thing by what is adjacent to it, as in their saying: "the gutter flowed" and "the river ran".
e- Al-munāsaba (correspondence): in the correspondence of the words to one another in measure, which is clear in the words آبائكم, إخوانكم, أعمامكم and أخوالكم.
[f-] [Translator's note: the source omits the letter for this item] Al-mathal (proverb): in His saying «ليس عليكم جناح أن تأكلوا جميعا وأشتاتا» [Translator's note: the source has «وأشتاتا»; the verse reads «أو أشتاتا»], which came out in the form of a current proverb that may properly be cited in every incident resembling its incident.
g- Al-tadhyīl (appended confirmation): the speech that came in the form of a proverb came as an appendix to the meaning of the preceding speech, with the purpose of emphasising and establishing it.
h- Al-muṭābaqa (antithesis): in His saying «جميعا أو أشتاتا», for these two words are opposed with an opposition that requires describing them as antithesis, since the meaning is "together or separately".
i- Al-muqārana (conjunction of devices): in two places. The first is the conjunction of proverbial illustration (tamthīl) with tadhyīl, as explained above; the second is the conjunction of antithesis with tamkīn (a well-settled ending), for the closing (fāṣila) of this speech is utterly well-settled.

* Benefits:
In the section on i'rab we mentioned the nearest view on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He, «لَيْسَ عَلَى الْأَعْمى حَرَجٌ» (the verse), and we promised you to set out the remaining views that the commentators mentioned. The believers used to take the weak and those with infirmities to the houses of their wives and children and to the houses of their relatives and friends, and feed them from them. A misgiving about that entered the hearts of those who fed and those who were fed, and they feared they might incur blame in it, and disliked that it be eating without right, because of His saying, Exalted is He, «وَلا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِالْباطِلِ». So it was said to them: there is no blame on the weak, nor on yourselves — meaning on you and on those of the believers in a state like yours — in that.
It is also said: they used to go out on campaigns and leave the weak behind in their houses, handing them the keys and permitting them to eat from their houses, but they would feel awkward. It is related of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr that he went out on a campaign and left Mālik ibn Zayd in charge of his house and wealth. When he returned he saw him exhausted and said: "What has befallen you?" He said: "I had nothing, and it was not lawful for me to eat from your wealth." So it was said to me [Translator's note: so in the source, «فقيل لي»]: there is no blame on these weak ones in what they felt awkward about, nor on you in eating from these houses.
It is also said that it was revealed as a dispensation for these [people] in staying behind from jihad. On this view, the statement is complete with His saying «ولا على الأعرج حرج ولا على المريض حرج».

dervis-irab:34-38.t:
* Vocabulary:
(كَمِشْكاةٍ): al-mishkāt is a niche that does not go through [the wall]. It is said to be the iron or lead [vessel] in which the oil is put; it is said to be the pillar on whose top the lamp is placed; and it is said to be the iron fitting from which the lantern is hung. In al-Qāmūs and its commentary: al-mishkāt is every niche that does not go through, and everything in or on which the lamp is placed. It is also said that mishkāt is an Ethiopian word Arabicised. More discussion of it will come in the section on rhetoric.
(زُجاجَةٍ): al-zujāj, with fatḥa, ḍamma or kasra on the zāy, is a transparent substance made from sand and alkali (al-qilā); the vessel or a piece of it is a zujāja, also with three possible vowels on the zāy. What is meant is a lantern of bright Syrian glass.
(دُرِّيٌّ): shining. With ḍamma on the dāl, without hamza and with doubling, it is a relative adjective (nisba) from al-durr (pearls); it is likened to it for its purity and brilliance. Its origin may also be with hamza, the hamza having been lightened; it is then fiʿʿīl from al-darʾ, which is [the star's] repelling the darkness by its light. It is read with kasra on the meaning of the second view, and it is then on the pattern fiʿʿīl, like sikkīt and ṣiddīq. In al-Mukhtār: "Al-darʾ is repelling, of the pattern of qaṭaʿa; daraʾa: it rose suddenly, of the pattern of khaḍaʿa; and from it is kawkab dirrīʾ, like sikkīt, for the intensity of its blazing and glittering. Durriyy with ḍamma is a nisba to al-durr. It has been read durrīʾ with ḍamma and hamza and darrīʾ with fatḥa and hamza. Tadāraʾtum: you pushed against one another and differed." In al-Asās: "Kawkab durriyy, and the darārī rose: they are related to al-dār [sic], which is the large pearls." And also in it: "Among the figurative usages: daraʾa al-kawkab: it rose as though it were repelling the darkness; and daraʾat al-nār: the fire shone."
[Translator's note: «الدار» in the al-Asās quotation is evidently a misprint for «الدرّ» (pearls).]
(الْآصالِ): plural of aṣīl, which is the time between ʿaṣr and maghrib; it is also pluralised as aṣāʾil, uṣul and uṣlān.

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ أَنْزَلْنا إِلَيْكُمْ آياتٍ مُبَيِّناتٍ وَمَثَلًا مِنَ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ وَمَوْعِظَةً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ): the wāw is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to set out the reality of the revealed verses. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of realisation (taḥqīq); أنزلنا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); إليكم is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) أنزلنا; آيات is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); مبينات is a naʿt (adjective), read with kasra or fatḥa on the yāʾ; ومثلا is conjoined to آيات; من الذين is a naʿt of مثلا; the clause خلوا is the ṣila (relative clause); من قبلكم is a ḥāl (circumstantial); وموعظة is conjoined to مثلا; للمتقين is a naʿt of موعظة.
(اللَّهُ نُورُ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ مَثَلُ نُورِهِ كَمِشْكاةٍ فِيها مِصْباحٌ): الله is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and نور السموات والأرض its khabar (predicate). مثل is a mubtadaʾ and نوره the muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct); the kāf is a noun meaning "like", the khabar, and مشكاة is its muḍāf ilayhi. The kāf may also be parsed as a preposition, the preposition and its genitive noun being the khabar of مثل. فيها is a fronted khabar and مصباح a postponed mubtadaʾ, the clause being a naʿt of مشكاة. Verification of this discourse will come in the section on rhetoric. The clause مثل نوره is an explanation of what precedes it, so it has no grammatical position.
(الْمِصْباحُ فِي زُجاجَةٍ): a mubtadaʾ and khabar; the clause is an explanation of what precedes it, so it has no grammatical position.
(الزُّجاجَةُ كَأَنَّها كَوْكَبٌ دُرِّيٌّ يُوقَدُ مِنْ شَجَرَةٍ مُبارَكَةٍ زَيْتُونَةٍ لا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلا غَرْبِيَّةٍ): الزجاجة is a mubtadaʾ; كأنّ and its noun; كوكب is its khabar and دري a naʿt of كوكب; the clause is the khabar of الزجاجة; the clause الزجاجة … is an explanation of what precedes it, so it has no grammatical position. The clause يوقد is a second naʿt of كوكب, and its nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent (mustatir). من شجرة is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يوقد; it is for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), with an omitted muḍāf, i.e. from the oil of a tree. مباركة is a naʿt of شجرة; زيتونة is a badal (substitute) of شجرة; لا شرقية is a second naʿt of شجرة — لا entered to convey negation, so it does not intervene between the qualifier and the qualified; ولا غربية is conjoined. More elucidation of this meaning will come in the section on rhetoric.
(يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ نُورٌ عَلى نُورٍ): this clause is a third naʿt of شجرة. يكاد is an incomplete (nāqiṣ) imperfect verb, one of the verbs of approximation; زيتها is its noun and the clause يضيء its khabar. ولو: the wāw is circumstantial and لو conditional; لم is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive government; تمسسه is an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by لم; the apodosis of لو is omitted, i.e. "it would shine", as indicated by what precedes it; the clause is a ḥāl, لو here conveying the exhaustion of all states, i.e. even in this state. نار is the agent of تمسسه. نور is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. this to which the Truth has been likened is a multiplied light; على نور is attached to an omitted naʿt of نور, emphasising it. The secret of the indefiniteness of نور will come in the section on rhetoric.
(يَهْدِي اللَّهُ لِنُورِهِ مَنْ يَشاءُ وَيَضْرِبُ اللَّهُ الْأَمْثالَ لِلنَّاسِ وَاللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ): the clause is resumptive, brought to establish the execution of His will, Glorified is He. لنوره is attached to يهدي; من يشاء is the object of يهدي; the clause يشاء is the ṣila; يضرب الله is an imperfect verb and its agent; الأمثال is the direct object; للناس is attached to يضرب. والله: the wāw is resumptive or a conjunction; الله is a mubtadaʾ; بكل شيء is attached to عليم; عليم is the khabar of الله.
(فِي بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ اللَّهُ أَنْ تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ): في بيوت is a naʿt of مشكاة, i.e. like a niche in houses, or of مصباح or of زجاجة; or it is attached to يوقد. On this [view] one does not pause at عليم. You may pause at عليم and attach it to an omitted [verb], its implied form being "glorify Him in houses", or to يسبّح. Ibn al-Anbārī said: I heard Abū al-ʿAbbās say: it is a ḥāl of the lamp, the glass and the star, as though it were said "and it is in houses". It is also said to be attached to توقد, i.e. it is lit in houses. The clause أذن الله is a naʿt of بيوت; أن and what follows it is accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "for (fī) their being raised"; ويذكر is conjoined to ترفع, in the passive; فيها is attached to يذكر; اسمه is the deputy agent.
(يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ فِيها بِالْغُدُوِّ وَالْآصالِ) (رِجالٌ لا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجارَةٌ وَلا بَيْعٌ عَنْ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَإِقامِ الصَّلاةِ وَإِيتاءِ الزَّكاةِ): the clause is a second naʿt of بيوت; له is attached to يسبح; بالغدو والآصال is a ḥāl; رجال is the agent of يسبح; the clause لا تلهيهم is a naʿt of رجال; تجارة is the agent of تلهيهم; ولا بيع is conjoined to تجارة; عن ذكر الله is attached to تلهيهم, and what follows it is conjoined to ذكر الله.
(يَخافُونَ يَوْماً تَتَقَلَّبُ فِيهِ الْقُلُوبُ وَالْأَبْصارُ): the clause is a second naʿt of رجال or a ḥāl of the object of تلهيهم. يخافون is a verb and its agent; يوما is a direct object, not an adverb; the clause تتقلب is a naʿt of يوما; فيه is attached to تتقلب; القلوب is the agent of تتقلب; والأبصار is conjoined to القلوب.
(لِيَجْزِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنَ ما عَمِلُوا وَيَزِيدَهُمْ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ): the lām is causal; يجزيهم is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after the causal lām; the hāʾ is the first direct object; الله is the agent; أحسن is the second direct object; ما is the muḍāf ilayhi; the clause عملوا is the ṣila; ويزيدهم is conjoined to ليجزيهم; من فضله is attached to يزيدهم.
(وَاللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَنْ يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ): the wāw is resumptive; الله is a mubtadaʾ and the clause يرزق the khabar; من is the direct object; the clause يشاء is the ṣila; بغير حساب is a ḥāl.
[Translator's note: the source prints «حلل» here, a misprint for «حال» (ḥāl); and «تنكسير» above for «تنكير» (indefiniteness).]

* Rhetoric:
These verses are filled with many varieties of rhetoric and eloquence, and we shall expand on them somewhat, following our practice in this book; we shall distribute these discussions in successive instalments.
1- The eloquent simile (al-tashbīh al-balīgh) in His words, Exalted is He, «اللَّهُ نُورُ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ»: what is meant is the simile whose particle [of comparison] is suppressed; it has been mentioned before with the divisions of simile. It is called "eloquent" only because of the omission of the mediating particle and its concision due to this omission. The scholars of rhetoric have spoken at length on this simile and tried to give concrete form to the manner in which it is permissible, because light, as is known, is a quality or accident perceived by sight, so it is not valid to predicate it of the Holy Essence. The best that is said about it is that the simile proceeds by way of bringing [the meaning] close to the mind, i.e. by Him, Exalted is He, and by His power the lights of heaven and earth shone and their affairs were set right, because the manifestation of existents came about through Him, just as all visible things come about through light. Or it is figurative, i.e. the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth; or by an implied muḍāf, as when you say "Zayd is justice", i.e. possessed of justice.
[Translator's note: the source has «ولو جازته» for «ولوجازته» (and its concision) and «ذو عدول» for the expected «ذو عدل»; translated by sense.]
2- The explicit simile (al-tashbīh al-mursal) in His words «مثل نوره كمشكاة فيها مصباح ...» — the verse. The simile here comes by means of the particle, namely the kāf. What is meant is that the light to which the Truth is likened is a multiplied light in which the niche, the glass, the lamp and the oil have competed [in support] until nothing remained that could strengthen the light. They differed over this simile: is it a representative (tamthīlī) simile, i.e. composite, in which the likening of a whole to a whole is intended without regard to matching part with part — the intent being to liken His guidance and His perfecting of His workmanship in every creature, as a whole, to this whole of light which you make use of, which is the most eloquent description of light known to you — or a non-representative simile, i.e. non-composite, in which matching part with part is intended? Al-Qurṭubī allowed both views; this is the text of his words:
"His words 'the likeness of His light', i.e. the description of His proofs which He casts into the believer's heart. Proofs are called light; Allah the Exalted called His Book a light, saying «وأنزلنا إليكم نورا مبينا» (and We sent down to you a clear light), and called His Prophet a light, saying «قد جاءكم من الله نور وكتاب مبين» (there has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book). This is because the Book guides and makes clear, and likewise the Messenger. The reason for the annexation to Allah the Exalted is that He is the establisher of the proof, its expounder and its maker. The verse bears another meaning in which there is no matching of a part of the likeness with a part of what it is likened to, but the simile is of a whole to a whole: namely that He means: the likeness of the light of Allah — which is His guidance, His perfecting of the workmanship of every creature, and His shining proofs as a whole — is like this whole of light which you make use of in this form, which is the most eloquent form of light that people have at hand. So the likeness of Allah's light in clarity is like this which is your utmost, O mankind."
Al-Karkhī excelled in his definition of this representative simile, saying:
"... Allah likened His light, i.e. knowledge of Him, in the believer's heart, to the light of a lamp rather than the light of the sun, although its light is more complete, because what is intended is to represent the light in the heart, the heart in the breast and the breast in the body, by the lamp, the lamp in the glass and the glass in the lantern; and this representation is only sound in what was mentioned. Or because the light of knowledge has instruments on whose combination it depends, such as the mind, understanding, intellect, wakefulness and others. And because the light of the sun shines directed towards the lower world, while the light of knowledge shines directed towards the upper world, like the light of a lamp. And because of the great benefit of oil and its being, for the most part, free of what mixes with it, the simile was made with its light rather than the light of a candle, although that is more complete than the light of a lamp."
[Translator's note: «تناحر فيه» is printed in the source; the context suggests «تناصر» (supported one another); rendered "competed [in support]".]
3- Antithesis (al-ṭibāq): in His words, Exalted is He, «لا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلا غَرْبِيَّةٍ». The scholars of rhetoric have spoken much about this antithesis and what is intended by it. Al-Zamakhsharī said:
"It is said: [it is] neither in a sunny spot (maḍḥā) nor in a shady spot (maqnaʾa) (which is the place on which the sun does not rise), but sun and shade alternate upon it, and that is better for its fruit and purer for its oil. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'There is no good in a tree in a shady spot, nor plants in a shady spot, and no good in them in a sunny spot.' It is also said: it is not among those on which the sun rises only at its rising or only at its setting; rather it reaches it in the morning and evening together, so it is both eastern and western."
Ibn al-Athīr has a subtle statement on this subject. He said: "As for the representation of the light of Allah the Exalted by a niche in which is a lamp, this is a likeness He struck for the Prophet ﷺ, as is indicated by His saying «توقد من شجرة مباركة زيتونة لا شرقية ولا غربية». If you consider this passage you will find it a subtle, wondrous simile: the heart of the Prophet ﷺ, the light cast into it and the transparent quality it has, are like the glass which is as though it were a star for its purity and brilliance. As for the blessed tree that is neither eastern nor western, it expresses the person of the Prophet ﷺ, because he is from the land of the Ḥijāz, which inclines neither to the east nor to the west. As for the oil of this glass, it shines without fire touching it; what is meant by that is that his natural disposition is pure of turbidity, luminous before meeting the lights."
4- Indefiniteness (al-tankīr): in the indefiniteness of His words «نور على نور» there is a kind of grandeur and hyperbole than which nothing is more elegant or beautiful. It is not one specific light, or a non-specific one, above another light like it; nor is it the sum of two lights only; rather it expresses a multiplied light, without limiting its multiplication to a fixed limit. This expression has captivated our Arab poets, and they have gazed at its heaven. Abū Tammām said, describing his exile in Egypt:
أخمسة أعوام مضت لمغيبه ... وشهران بل يومان ثكل على ثكل
(Five years have passed since his absence, and two months — nay, two days: bereavement upon bereavement.)
Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī said:
أرق على أرق ومثلي يأرق ... وجوى يزيد وعبرة تترقرق
(Sleeplessness upon sleeplessness — and one like me does lie awake — and a passion that grows, and a tear that wells up.)
And Shawqī said in the modern age, lamenting the late Fawzī al-Ghazzī, one of the notables of Damascus:
جرح على جرح حنانك جلق ... حملت ما يوهي الجبال ويرهق
(Wound upon wound — mercy, Jilliq [Damascus]! You have borne what would weaken and exhaust the mountains.)
5- Similarity of the extremities (tashābuh al-aṭrāf): this is that the speaker looks to a word that occurs at the end of a clause of a passage in prose, or the last word at the end of the first hemistich in verse, and begins with it ... Consider the similarity of the extremities of these successive clauses: «الله نور السموات والأرض، مثل نوره كمشكاة فيها مصباح، المصباح في زجاجة، الزجاجة كأنه كوكب دري». Among examples in poetry is the saying of Laylā al-Akhyaliyya about al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf:
إذا نزل الحجاج أرضا مريضة ... تتبع أقصى دائها فشفاها
شفاها من الداء العضال الذي بها ... غلام إذا هز القناة سقاها
سقاها فرواها بشرب سجاله ... دماء رجال يحلبون حراها
(When al-Ḥajjāj alights on a sick land he traces its deepest disease and cures it; he cures it of the incurable disease within it — a young man who, when he brandishes the spear, gives it to drink; he gives it to drink and quenches it with draughts from his buckets: the blood of men who milk its udders.)
[Translator's note: the source quotes the Qur'anic «كأنها» as «كأنه», and prints these verses (and those of Abū Nuwās below) with displaced line divisions («س / قاها»); they are given here in verse order without changing the words.]
And beautiful is the saying of Abū Tammām:
هوى كان خلسا إن من أبرد الهوى ... هوى جلت في افنائه وهو خامل
أبا جعفر إنّ الجهالة أمها ... ولود وأم العلم حذاء حائل
فكن هضبة نأوى إليها وحرة ... يعدد عنها الاعوجي المناقل
فإن الفتى في كل ضرب مناسب ... مناسب روحانية من يشاكل
(A love that was snatched — the coolest love is a love in whose precincts you roamed while it was obscure. O Abū Jaʿfar, the mother of ignorance is prolific, while the mother of knowledge is short-lived and barren. So be a hill we take refuge in, and a rugged lava-field from which the fleet-footed Aʿwajī steed turns away. For the young man, in every kind, has spiritual kinship with whoever resembles him.)
And attributed to Abū Nuwās is his saying:
خزيمة خير بني حازم ... وحازم خير بني دارم
ودارم خير تميم وما ... مثل تميم في بني آدم
إلا البهاليل بني هاشم ... وهم سيوف لبني هاشم
(Khuzayma is the best of Banū Ḥāzim, and Ḥāzim the best of Banū Dārim, and Dārim the best of Tamīm, and there is none like Tamīm among the sons of Adam except the noble lords of Banū Hāshim — and they are swords for Banū Hāshim.)
The similarity of extremities may also be in meaning: that the speaker ends his speech with what corresponds to its beginning in meaning, not in wording, as in the saying of Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Salāmī:
بدائع الحسن فيه مفترقه ... وأعين الناس فيه متفقة
سهام ألحاظه مفوقه ... فكل من رام لحظه رشقه
قد كتب الحسن فوق عارضه ... هذا مليح وحق من خلقه
(The wonders of beauty are dispersed in him, and people's eyes agree upon him; the arrows of his glances are notched ready, so whoever seeks to glance at him, he shoots him; beauty has written above his cheek: "This is lovely — by the truth of Him who created him.")
So the shooting (al-rashq) in the rhyme of the second verse corresponds to the arrows at its beginning.
And beautiful is the saying of al-Sarī al-Raffāʾ:
ابريقنا عاكف على قدح ... كأنه الأم ترفع الولدا
أو عابد من بني المجوس إذا ... توهم الكأس شعلة سجدا
(Our ewer stoops over a cup as though it were a mother lifting her child, or a worshipper of the Magians who, when he fancies the goblet a flame, prostrates.)
So prostration corresponds to the worshipper at the beginning of the verse.
And Ibn al-Rūmī reached the utmost in describing a singing-girl:
جاءت بوجه كأنه قمر ... على قوام كأنه غصن
غنت فلم تبق فيّ جارحة ... إلا تمنيت أنها أذن
(She came with a face like a moon upon a stature like a bough; she sang, and no limb remained in me but I wished it were an ear.)
So the ear corresponds to the mention of singing at the beginning of the verse.
A correction of some critics:
The secrets of the similarity of extremities were hidden from one of the scholars of rhetoric, who asserted that if a word is mentioned at the beginning of speech that needs completion, it should be repeated identically at its end, and whenever one departs from this it is faulty. He then illustrated this with a saying of Abū Tammām and a saying of Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī, saying that Abū Tammām erred in his saying:
بسط الرجاء لنا برغم نوائب ... كثرت بهن مصارع الآمال
(He spread out hope for us, in spite of calamities through which the deaths of hopes have multiplied.)
For since he mentioned al-rajāʾ (hope) at the opening of the verse, he should have repeated its mention at its close as well, or mentioned al-āmāl (hopes) at both opening and close. Likewise Abū al-Ṭayyib erred in his saying:
اني لأعلم واللبيب خبير ... أن الحياة وان حرصت غرور
(I know — and the intelligent man is well-informed — that life, however eager you are for it, is a delusion.)
For he said «إني لأعلم واللبيب خبير», and he should have said «إني لأعلم واللبيب عليم», so that it would be a correct correspondence.
[Translator's note: the source prints «الي لأعلم», a misprint for «إني لأعلم».]
This is what the critic mentioned, and it is worth nothing, because what is relied upon in this regard is that if the word has the meaning of its sister-word, it is permissible.
6- Rational (cognitive) metaphor (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī): in His words «يخافون يوما تتقلب فيه القلوب والأبصار», turning over and agitation from terror and fright are attributed to the hearts and the eyes.
And in His words «يكاد زيتها يضيء ولو لم تمسسه نار» there is the device of extravagance (al-ghuluww), which is going to excess in describing a thing that is impossible both rationally and customarily. It is divided into two kinds, acceptable and unacceptable. In the acceptable kind, the poet must bring it close to acceptance by a particle of approximation — unless the extravagance is in praise of the Prophet ﷺ, in which case there is no extravagance. The poet must cast it in the mould of imaginings that invite the mind to accept them at first glance, like the noble verse: the oil's shining without fire touching it is rationally impossible, but the word يكاد (almost) brought it near, so it became acceptable.
The second kind is unacceptable extravagance, as in the saying of Abū Nuwās:
وأخفت أهل الشرك حتى أنه ... لتخافك النطف التي لم تخلق
(You have so terrified the people of polytheism that the sperm-drops not yet created fear you.)

dervis-irab:62-64.t:
* Vocabulary:
(يَتَسَلَّلُونَ): they slip away one after another, or little by little.
(لِواذاً): In al-Qāmūs: "al-lawdh bil-shayʾ is taking cover and shelter in it, like al-liwādh — [with the lām vowelled] in three ways — al-liyādh and al-mulāwadha; [it also means] encompassing, like al-ilādha; the side of a mountain and what surrounds it; and the bend of a valley; the plural is alwādh." The hypocrites used to go out, screening themselves behind people, without asking permission, so as not to be seen. [It is of the form] mufāʿala because each of them takes cover behind his companion, so the sharing is present. The wāw in (لواذا) remained sound despite the kasra before it only because it is sound in the verb, which is lāwadha; had it been the maṣdar (verbal noun) of lādha, it would be liyādh, like ṣāma ṣiyāman and qāma qiyāman.
(يُخالِفُونَ): It is said "khālafahu ilā al-amr" when he went to it instead of him, and "khālafahu ʿan al-amr" when he turned away from it instead of him.

* I'rab:
(إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ) A resumptive clause set out to establish the state of the hypocrites, at whom the Prophet used to hint in his assemblies and sermons.
(إنما) is the restraining (kāffa) and restrained (makfūfa) particle; (المؤمنون) is the mubtadaʾ (subject) and (الذين) its khabar (predicate); the clause (آمنوا بالله ورسوله) is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun, i.e. these are the believers perfect in faith. As for the hypocrites, when they sat in his assembly they would watch his Companions furtively, and if any inattention towards them appeared on their part, they slipped away under cover and left secretly without asking permission.
(وَإِذا كانُوا مَعَهُ عَلى أَمْرٍ جامِعٍ لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا حَتَّى يَسْتَأْذِنُوهُ) The wāw is a conjunction; (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition; the clause (كانوا) is in the position of genitive by the adverb's being annexed to it; the wāw is the noun of kāna; (معه) is an adverb attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar; (على أمر) is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial) — and you may reverse the matter. (جامع) is an adjective of (أمر), such as wars, the Friday prayer and the two ʿĪd prayers; the meaning of attributing "gathering" to the matter will come in the section on rhetoric. The clause (لم يذهبوا) has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) of a non-jussive condition. (حتى) is a particle of limit and a preposition; (يستأذنوه) is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied «أن» after (حتى); (يستأذنوه) is a verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object). (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَأْذِنُونَكَ أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ) Inna and its noun; the clause (يستأذنونك) is the ṣila; (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ and (الذين) its khabar; the clause (يؤمنون بالله ورسوله) is the ṣila of the relative noun; and the nominal clause is the khabar of inna. (فَإِذَا اسْتَأْذَنُوكَ لِبَعْضِ شَأْنِهِمْ فَأْذَنْ لِمَنْ شِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the sense of a condition; the clause (استأذنوك) is genitive by the adverb's being annexed to it; (لبعض شأنهم) is attached to (استأذنوك), serving as the reason for asking permission. (فائذن): the fāʾ links the answer of (إذا); (ائذن) is an imperative verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; (لمن) is attached to it; the clause (شئت) is the ṣila; (منهم) is a ḥāl. In it is the delegation of the matter to the judgement of the Messenger of Allah. (وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمُ اللَّهَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ) (واستغفر) is conjoined to (فائذن); (لهم) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (استغفر); the clause (إن الله غفور رحيم) gives the reason for asking forgiveness, so it has no grammatical position. (لا تَجْعَلُوا دُعاءَ الرَّسُولِ بَيْنَكُمْ كَدُعاءِ بَعْضِكُمْ بَعْضاً) The commentators' statements are in disarray over the interpretation of this expression. The nearest of what has been said about it is: do not make his calling you like the calling of some of you to others, so that you dawdle and hold back as some of you dawdle and hold back from others when one calls him for a matter. So the maṣdar, which is (دعاء), is annexed to the agent. It may also be annexed to the object, i.e. your calling the Messenger and your addressing him [should not be] like the calling and addressing of some of you to others. (لا) is prohibitive; (تجعلوا) is an imperfect verb made jussive by the prohibitive (لا); the wāw is the fāʿil; (دعاء الرسول) is the direct object; (بينكم) is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl; the kāf, in the sense of «مثل», is the second direct object; (بعضكم) is annexed to (دعاء) [as muḍāf ilayhi]; and (بعضا) is the direct object of (دعاء). Some made it accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. "to some" (li-baʿḍ), and that is necessary when (دعاء) is taken as annexed to its object.
(قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ يَتَسَلَّلُونَ مِنْكُمْ لِواذاً) (قد) here has the meaning of «ربما», and that is regular when it enters the imperfect; more detail about it will come in the section on benefits. (يعلم الله) is an imperfect verb and its agent; the clause (يتسللون) is the ṣila; (منكم) is attached to (يتسللون). (لواذا) may be accusative as a maṣdar from the meaning of the verb, if the implied sense is "they slip away from you a slipping away" or "they take cover a taking cover"; and it may be a maṣdar in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. "taking cover" (mulāwidhīn). (فَلْيَحْذَرِ الَّذِينَ يُخالِفُونَ عَنْ أَمْرِهِ أَنْ تُصِيبَهُمْ فِتْنَةٌ أَوْ يُصِيبَهُمْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ) The fāʾ is the faṣīḥa (the fāʾ implying an omitted condition), or a conjunction [conjoining] to «قد يعلم», because it is consequent upon it. The lām is the lām of command; (يحذر) is an imperfect verb made jussive by the lām of command; (الذين) is the fāʿil; the clause (يخالفون) is the ṣila. The object of (يخالفون) is omitted, and it is Allah the Exalted, because He is the one who commands. «عن» was brought because it [the verb] contains the meaning of turning away and aversion. (أن يصيبهم) is the object of (يحذر); (فتنة) is the fāʿil; and (أو يصيبهم عذاب أليم) is conjoined to (أن تصيبهم فتنة). (أَلا إِنَّ لِلَّهِ ما فِي السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ قَدْ يَعْلَمُ ما أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ) (قد) is for frequency (taktīr), as preceded and as will come. (يعلم) is an imperfect verb with a latent agent referring to Allah the Exalted; (ما) is the direct object; (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ and (عليه) the khabar, and the clause is the ṣila. (وَيَوْمَ يُرْجَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ فَيُنَبِّئُهُمْ بِما عَمِلُوا وَاللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ) (ويوم) is conjoined to the object of (يعلم), i.e. "and He knows what they are returned" [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense is "and He knows the day on which they are returned"]. The clause (يرجعون) is the ṣila [Translator's note: so in the source; it is more usually parsed as genitive by the annexation of (يوم) to it]; (يرجعون) is with the passive form. (فينبئهم) is conjoined to (يعلم); the hāʾ is the object; (بما عملوا) is in the position of the second object. (الله) is a mubtadaʾ; (بكل شيء) is attached to (عليم), and (عليم) is the khabar.

* Benefits:
The discussion of «قد» has preceded, and we add here that when it enters the imperfect it conveys frequency (taktīr) and has the meaning of «ربما». Of this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā:
أخي ثقة لا تهلك الخمر ماله ... ولكنه قد يهلك المال نائله
(A trustworthy man, whose wealth wine does not destroy; rather, his giving often destroys his wealth.)
«قد» here is for frequency; otherwise it would not be praise. Al-thiqa is from wathiqa, like al-ʿida from waʿada. Attributing destruction to wine is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), and likewise attributing it to al-nāʾil, i.e. giving; what is meant is describing him with generosity. Among the examples of «ربما» is the saying of Ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Sindī elegising Ibn Hubayra:
ألا إن عينا لم تجد يوم واسط ... عليك بجاري دمعها لجمود
عشية قام النائحات وشققت ... جيوب بأيدي مأتم وخدود
فإن تمس مهجور الفناء فربما ... أقام به بعد الوفود وفود
